```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

import json
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.dates as mdates
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as ticker
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import HTML

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)

POST_DIR = Path(".").resolve()
CLEAN_DIR = POST_DIR / "data" / "clean"
IMG_DIR = POST_DIR / "images"
STATS_DIR = POST_DIR / "stats"
IMG_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

with open(STATS_DIR / "summary_stats.json", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    stats = json.load(handle)

labor = pd.read_csv(CLEAN_DIR / "labor_monthly.csv", index_col="date", parse_dates=True).sort_index()
sector = pd.read_csv(CLEAN_DIR / "sector_august.csv")

COLORS = {
    "primary": "#2e5984",
    "accent": "#8b0000",
    "secondary": "#6b8e6b",
    "neutral": "#4a4a4a",
    "light": "#b0b0b0",
    "warning": "#cc7722",
    "fed_target": "#cc0000",
    "recession": "#888888",
}

plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.family": "Calibri",
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 8,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": False,
    "axes.linewidth": 0.5,
    "lines.linewidth": 1.8,
    "figure.facecolor": "white",
    "axes.facecolor": "#fafafa",
    "figure.dpi": 100,
})


def fmt(value, digits=1):
    return f"{float(value):.{digits}f}"


def fmt_chg(value, digits=1):
    return f"{float(value):+.{digits}f}"


def fmt2(value):
    return f"{float(value):.2f}"


def extend_xlim(ax, index, pad_frac=0.12):
    span = index[-1] - index[0]
    ax.set_xlim(index[0], index[-1] + span * pad_frac)
```

The August jobs report was a beat, not a boom. Nonfarm payrolls rose `{python} fmt_chg(stats['payroll_aug_k'], 0)`k, against a [Wall Street Journal survey of economists](https://www.wsj.com/economy/jobs/august-jobs-report-unemployment-c9da2f0c) at +53k and a prior-12-month average of `{python} fmt_chg(stats['prior_12m_avg_k'], 0)`k. The Bureau of Labor Statistics also revised June and July up by a combined `{python} fmt_chg(stats['combined_revision_k'], 0)`k, so July's first-print scare is smaller than it looked.

The catch is composition. Food services and drinking places plus local government education supplied `{python} fmt(stats['two_sector_share_pct'])`% of the monthly gain. Average hourly earnings rose `{python} fmt(stats['ahe_mom_pct'])`% on the month and `{python} fmt(stats['ahe_yoy_pct'])`% over the year. That is a labor market that hired in restaurants and schools after a weak July - not one that suddenly tightened heading into the `{python} stats['next_fomc_date']` FOMC.

Establishment payrolls and the household survey are separate samples. JOLTS (Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey) and claims in this post are lagged and prose-only.

## Headline payrolls and revisions

Total nonfarm payrolls rose `{python} fmt_chg(stats['payroll_aug_k'], 0)`k in August. Private payrolls rose `{python} fmt_chg(stats['private_aug_k'], 0)`k and government added `{python} fmt_chg(stats['government_aug_k'], 0)`k. That is a step up from the first July print of `{python} fmt_chg(stats['july_initial_k'], 0)`k, which BLS later revised to `{python} fmt_chg(stats['july_revised_k'], 0)`k.

The revision math matters as much as the new month. June moved from `{python} fmt_chg(stats['june_initial_k'], 0)`k to `{python} fmt_chg(stats['june_revised_k'], 0)`k. July moved up by `{python} fmt_chg(stats['july_revision_k'], 0)`k. Together those two months are `{python} fmt_chg(stats['combined_revision_k'], 0)`k stronger than first reported.

The prior 12-month average was `{python} fmt_chg(stats['prior_12m_avg_k'], 0)`k. The three-month average, which now includes August, is `{python} fmt_chg(stats['payroll_3m_avg_k'], 0)`k. Hiring improved. The trend is still modest.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-payroll-path
#| fig-cap: "August nonfarm payrolls jumped to +162k, well above the prior 12-month average, after a weak July that was later revised up."

# Monthly payroll change comes from scripts/02_clean_data.py (this month's
# PAYEMS level minus last month's). The three-month line is a simple mean
# of those changes, not an annualized rate.
plot = labor.loc["2024-01-01":].copy()
bar_colors = np.where(plot["payems_chg"] >= 0, COLORS["primary"], COLORS["accent"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.6))
ax.bar(plot.index, plot["payems_chg"], width=20, color=bar_colors, alpha=0.7, edgecolor="white")
ax.plot(
    plot.index,
    plot["payroll_3m_avg"],
    color=COLORS["warning"],
    linewidth=1.8,
    label="Three-month average",
)
ax.axhline(0, color=COLORS["neutral"], linewidth=0.8)
ax.axhline(
    stats["prior_12m_avg_k"],
    color=COLORS["neutral"],
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=0.8,
    alpha=0.8,
    label="Prior 12-month average",
)

last_date = plot.index[-1]
last_value = plot["payems_chg"].iloc[-1]
ax.scatter(
    last_date,
    last_value,
    s=40,
    color=COLORS["primary"],
    zorder=5,
    edgecolors="white",
    linewidth=0.8,
)
ax.text(
    last_date,
```

The three-month average is still well below the early-2024 hiring pace on this chart.

## The rebound was concentrated

Food services and drinking places added `{python} fmt_chg(stats['food_services_aug_k'], 0)`k jobs, versus a `{python} fmt_chg(stats['food_services_12m_avg_k'], 0)`k average over the prior 12 months. Local government education added `{python} fmt_chg(stats['local_education_aug_k'], 0)`k, after `{python} fmt_chg(stats['local_education_jul_k'], 0)`k in July. Those two categories sum to `{python} fmt_chg(stats['two_sector_sum_k'], 0)`k, or `{python} fmt(stats['two_sector_share_pct'])`% of the `{python} fmt_chg(stats['payroll_aug_k'], 0)`k total.

Construction added `{python} fmt_chg(stats['construction_aug_k'], 0)`k. Manufacturing added `{python} fmt_chg(stats['manufacturing_aug_k'], 0)`k and is up `{python} fmt_chg(stats['manufacturing_since_dec_k'], 0)`k since `{python} stats['manufacturing_low_month']`. Health care added `{python} fmt_chg(stats['healthcare_aug_k'], 0)`k, slower than its `{python} fmt_chg(stats['healthcare_12m_avg_k'], 0)`k prior-year pace. Information lost `{python} fmt(abs(stats['information_aug_k']), 0)`k jobs, worse than its `{python} fmt_chg(stats['information_12m_avg_k'], 0)`k average over the prior 12 months. That cut is the white-collar side of the story: restaurants and schools hired, while computing, publishing, and broadcasting did not.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-sector-mix
#| fig-cap: "Food services and local government education accounted for most of the August payroll gain, while information lost 23k jobs."

# August industry changes are first differences of CES levels from

# industries, so the bars sum to the headline payroll change.
plot_sector = sector.sort_values("change_k")
highlight = {"Food services", "Local gov education"}
bar_colors = []
for industry, value in zip(plot_sector["industry"], plot_sector["change_k"]):
    if value < 0:
        bar_colors.append(COLORS["accent"])
    elif industry in highlight:
        bar_colors.append(COLORS["primary"])

        bar_colors.append(COLORS["light"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.2))
ax.barh(
    plot_sector["industry"],
    plot_sector["change_k"],
    color=bar_colors,
    edgecolor="white",
    height=0.65,
)
x_span = plot_sector["change_k"].max() - plot_sector["change_k"].min()
for industry, value in zip(plot_sector["industry"], plot_sector["change_k"]):
    offset = 0.02 * x_span
    if value >= 0:
        ax.text(
            value + offset,
            industry,
            f"+{value:.0f}k",
            va="center",
            fontsize=8,
            color=COLORS["neutral"],

            value - offset,

            f"{value:.0f}k",

            color=COLORS["neutral"],
        )
ax.axvline(0, color=COLORS["neutral"], linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("August change, thousands")
ax.set_xlim(plot_sector["change_k"].min() - 12, plot_sector["change_k"].max() + 18)
```

Source: [BLS CES via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/), series CES7072200001, CES9093161101, USCONS, MANEMP, CES6562000101, USINFO, and PAYEMS.

Leisure and hospitality is the broader grouping that includes food services. It rose `{python} fmt_chg(stats['leisure_aug_k'], 0)`k, and food services accounted for `{python} fmt(stats['food_share_of_leisure_pct'])`% of that gain.

## Narrow gains over recent months

A one-month industry mix can be noise. The next check is whether food services plus local education, versus everything else, has been carrying recent payrolls. In August the two highlighted industries added `{python} fmt_chg(stats['two_sector_sum_k'], 0)`k after `{python} fmt_chg(stats['two_sector_jul_k'], 0)`k in July. The rest of payrolls added `{python} fmt_chg(stats['rest_aug_k'], 0)`k, down from `{python} fmt_chg(stats['rest_jul_k'], 0)`k in July.

That split is the reason the rebound can be real and still incomplete. The August bounce is a reversal in two concentrated industries, not a pickup in the rest of the economy. If restaurants and local school systems are doing the hiring, the print says less about factories, warehouses, professional services, and information than the headline suggests. Local education also has a seasonal fingerprint around the school year, even after seasonal adjustment, so one strong month there should not be read as a new public-sector boom.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-concentration
#| fig-cap: "Food services plus local government education, not the rest of the economy, produced most of August's payroll rebound."

# two_sector_chg is food services plus local government education.
# rest_chg is PAYEMS minus that sum. Both are built in 02_clean_data.py.
plot = labor.loc["2025-03-01":].copy()
x = np.arange(len(plot))
width = 0.38

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.6))
ax.bar(
    x - width / 2,
    plot["two_sector_chg"],
    width,
    color=COLORS["primary"],
    edgecolor="white",
    label="Food services + local education",
)
ax.bar(
    x + width / 2,
    plot["rest_chg"],
    width,
    color=COLORS["light"],
    edgecolor="white",
    label="Rest of payrolls",
)
ax.axhline(0, color=COLORS["neutral"], linewidth=0.8)

last = len(plot) - 1
ax.text(
    last - width / 2,
    plot["two_sector_chg"].iloc[-1] + 6,
    f"{plot['two_sector_chg'].iloc[-1]:+.0f}k",
    ha="center",
    fontsize=8,
    color=COLORS["primary"],
    fontweight="bold",
)
ax.text(
    last + width / 2,
    plot["rest_chg"].iloc[-1] + 6,
    f"{plot['rest_chg'].iloc[-1]:+.0f}k",
    ha="center",
    fontsize=8,
    color=COLORS["neutral"],
    fontweight="bold",
)

tick_idx = list(range(0, len(plot), 3))
ax.set_xticks(tick_idx)
ax.set_xticklabels([d.strftime("%b\n%Y") for d in plot.index[tick_idx]])
ax.set_ylabel("Monthly change, thousands")
ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda v, pos: f"{v:+.0f}"))
y_min = min(plot["two_sector_chg"].min(), plot["rest_chg"].min())
y_max = max(plot["two_sector_chg"].max(), plot["rest_chg"].max())
ax.set_ylim(y_min - 20, y_max + 35)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(IMG_DIR / "august-concentration.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
```

## Household survey: unemployment steady, participation up

The household survey asks people whether they are employed, unemployed, or outside the labor force. The unemployment rate (U-3) is the share of that labor force that is jobless and looking. It stayed at `{python} fmt(stats['unrate_aug'])`%, unchanged from July. U-6, a broader slack measure that adds marginally attached workers and people who want full-time hours but work part time, fell to `{python} fmt(stats['u6_aug'])`% from `{python} fmt(stats['u6_jul'])`%. U-6 is prose-only.

The labor-force participation rate is the share of adults who are working or looking. It rose to `{python} fmt(stats['participation_aug'])`% from `{python} fmt(stats['participation_jul'])`%. That is still `{python} fmt(abs(stats['participation_change_since_jan_pp']))` percentage point below January. The employment-population ratio, the share of adults with a job, rose to `{python} fmt(stats['emp_pop_aug'])`% from `{python} fmt(stats['emp_pop_jul'])`%. The labor force increased `{python} fmt_chg(stats['labor_force_chg_k'], 0)`k, employment rose `{python} fmt_chg(stats['employed_chg_k'], 0)`k, and the number of people not in the labor force fell `{python} fmt_chg(stats['nilf_chg_k'], 0)`k.

The two surveys measure different things. The establishment survey counts jobs on payrolls. The household survey counts people. They can disagree by hundreds of thousands in one month without either being wrong. August is a large disagreement: payrolls `{python} fmt_chg(stats['payroll_aug_k'], 0)`k, household employment `{python} fmt_chg(stats['employed_chg_k'], 0)`k, labor force `{python} fmt_chg(stats['labor_force_chg_k'], 0)`k. Use payrolls for the monthly hiring story. That survey has the larger sample, and it is the series the Fed and markets quote. Use the household survey for unemployment, participation, and labor-force entry. A one-month household surge does not license a tight-market read while U-3 is `{python} fmt(stats['unrate_aug'])`% and participation is still below January.

People working part time for economic reasons fell `{python} fmt_chg(stats['pte_economic_chg_k'], 0)`k to `{python} fmt(stats['pte_economic_m'])` million. The number of unemployed people was `{python} fmt(stats['unemployed_level_m'])` million.

## Wages and hours stayed moderate

Pay is the channel from a strong labor market into inflation. Average hourly earnings for all private employees rose `{python} fmt(stats['ahe_mom_cents'], 0)` cents, or `{python} fmt(stats['ahe_mom_pct'])`%, to `{python} fmt2(stats['ahe_level'])` dollars. Over the year they are up `{python} fmt(stats['ahe_yoy_pct'])`%. Production and nonsupervisory workers earned `{python} fmt2(stats['ahe_prod_level'])` dollars, up `{python} fmt(stats['ahe_prod_mom_cents'], 0)` cents, or `{python} fmt(stats['ahe_prod_mom_pct'])`%, on the month.

Hours edged up by `{python} fmt(stats['hours_chg'])` hour to `{python} fmt(stats['hours_level'])` from `{python} fmt(stats['hours_prev'])`. A labor market adding jobs in restaurants and local schools, with pay still rising `{python} fmt(stats['ahe_yoy_pct'])`% a year and the workweek at `{python} fmt(stats['hours_level'])` hours, is not a wage-spiral setup.

```{python}

)
axes[1].set_ylabel("Average weekly hours")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Month")
axes[1].set_ylim(33.5, 35.0)

for ax in axes:
    extend_xlim(ax, plot.index, 0.18)
    ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator())
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y"))

plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(IMG_DIR / "august-wages-hours.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
```

::: {.figure-source}
Source: [BLS CES via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/), CES0500000003 and AWHAETP.
:::

Yearly wage growth stayed moderate, and the workweek barely moved.

## Putting it together

August improved the labor picture after a weak July, and after June and July first prints that were later revised up. Payrolls rose `{python} fmt_chg(stats['payroll_aug_k'], 0)`k and revisions added `{python} fmt_chg(stats['combined_revision_k'], 0)`k. Most of the new jobs were in restaurants and local schools. Information lost jobs. Pay rose `{python} fmt(stats['ahe_yoy_pct'])`% over the year. The three-month payroll average is only `{python} fmt_chg(stats['payroll_3m_avg_k'], 0)`k. That is not a broken labor market, and it is not a broad boom.

### What it means for

- **For the Fed:** August takes the July-collapse scare off the table and puts almost no new tightness on it once restaurants and local schools are stripped out. This print alone does not force a September hike and does not revive an easing-on-labor-weakness story. **CPI on `{python} stats['next_cpi_date']` decides** whether officials treat labor as a constraint.
- **For households:** More people are working or looking than in July. Unemployment did not rise. Hiring is uneven. Information cut `{python} fmt(abs(stats['information_aug_k']), 0)`k jobs.
- **For investors:** Trade the quality of the gain, the `{python} fmt_chg(stats['combined_revision_k'], 0)`k revisions, and `{python} fmt(stats['ahe_yoy_pct'])`% wage growth not the headline.
- **For insurers:** Average hourly earnings up `{python} fmt(stats['ahe_yoy_pct'])`%, with hiring concentrated in food services, is not a broad jump in claim severity. Restaurant wage pressure matters more for that workers' compensation class than for professional services. Hours only edged up `{python} fmt(stats['hours_chg'])` to `{python} fmt(stats['hours_level'])`. That is directional only, not a pricing recommendation.

## What to watch next

- CPI on `{python} stats['next_cpi_date']`, before the FOMC.
- The FOMC decision on `{python} stats['next_fomc_date']`.
- The next Employment Situation on `{python} stats['next_jobs_date']`, including whether the rest of payrolls starts leading, not only whether restaurants and schools keep printing.
- JOLTS after `{python} stats['jolts_openings_month']` (latest openings `{python} fmt(stats['jolts_openings_m'])` million, quits rate `{python} fmt(stats['jolts_quits_rate'])`%, both prose-only) and weekly claims, last `{python} fmt(stats['claims_latest_k'], 0)`k as of `{python} stats['claims_as_of']`.

August hired. Most of the economy did not lead. The labor market can add `{python} fmt(stats['payroll_aug_k'], 0)`,000 jobs and still not be the market the Fed was afraid of in 2022.

## Limitations

- August payrolls are preliminary and will be revised twice.
- FRED stores the current CES vintage, so June and July first prints come from the BLS release text, not from a vintage database.
- The household and establishment surveys can diverge because they ask different questions of different samples. They can move in the same direction without matching month to month.
- Seasonal adjustment around the school year can move local government education more than other categories.
- JOLTS lags the jobs print and is not an August reading in this file. The latest JOLTS month here is `{python} stats['jolts_openings_month']`. Initial claims are weekly and also prose-only, current as of `{python} stats['claims_as_of']`.

### How this post was built

The Python pipeline and every chart block are in this post folder. Expand a chart block to see the code. Run the scripts in numeric order from this directory, then render `index.qmd`:

- `scripts/01_fetch_data.py` downloads validated FRED series for payrolls, household labor-market rates, wages, hours, and the highlighted industries.
- `scripts/02_clean_data.py` turns those levels into monthly job changes and percent rates. The formulas live there; the charts only plot the columns.
- `scripts/04_compute_stats.py` writes every figure used in the prose and metric cards to `stats/summary_stats.json`.

pandas handles the tables and matplotlib draws the figures. FRED already carried the `{python} stats['latest_month']` CES and CPS prints as of `{python} stats['bls_release_date']`. First-print June and July payroll figures that FRED does not store as a vintage are entered from the [BLS Employment Situation](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/empsit.nr0.htm) and marked `# MANUAL:` in `04_compute_stats.py`.
